Order Pholidota · Family Manidae

Pangolins: armored,
ant-eating, and endangered

Pangolins are super cool and awesome.

The only mammals wholly covered in scales are also some of the most trafficked wild animals on Earth. Here is what they are, how they live, and what's being done to save them.

01 · Introduction

What is a pangolin?

Pangolins look like reptiles or walking pinecones, but they are mammals: warm-blooded, with fur on their bellies, and they nurse their young.

They are the only mammals wholly covered in scales.5 All living pangolins belong to the family Manidae, the only family in the order Pholidota.6 They resemble anteaters and armadillos, but those animals aren't their closest relatives. Pangolins are most closely related to the carnivores (cats, dogs, bears and their kin), and the two lineages split almost 80 million years ago.56

There are eight recognized species, four in Asia and four in sub-Saharan Africa.16 They range in size from about 1.6 kg (3.5 lb)6 up to the giant pangolin, whose adults weigh more than 30 kg.1 In Cantonese their name means "the animal that digs through the mountain."6

MammalInsectivoreMostly nocturnalSolitaryNo teeth
02 · Anatomy

Built like a living suit of armor

A pangolin's body is specialized for two jobs: breaking into ant and termite nests, and surviving a predator's attack.

Keratin scales

The scales are made of keratin, the same protein as human hair and fingernails. They overlap like artichoke leaves and keep growing for the animal's whole life, while digging wears their edges down.6 Together they make up roughly 20% of body weight.3

An extraordinary tongue

The tongue is long, muscular, and sticky. It is anchored deep in the body near the pelvis and the last pair of ribs.6 In some pangolins it can reach lengths greater than the animal's own body.5

No teeth, a "gizzard" stomach

Pangolins have no teeth. Instead, a muscular stomach lined with keratin spines, usually holding small stones, mashes and grinds their prey, much like a bird's gizzard.6

Digging claws

Each forefoot has three long, curved claws for tearing open nests and digging burrows. To protect them, pangolins walk on the outer edges of their forefeet with the claws tucked underneath.6

Nose over eyes

Their eyesight is poor, so they find ant and termite nests by smell. Special muscles seal their nostrils and ears shut to keep biting insects out.6

The defensive ball

When threatened, a pangolin curls into a tight ball with its sharp-edged scales facing out.3 It may also hiss, puff, and lash its tail.6 The ball protects against many predators, but a curled-up pangolin is easy for a person to simply pick up.

Scales start soft

Newborns are about 15 cm (6 in) long and weigh about 340 g (12 oz). Their scales are soft and pale at birth and begin to harden by the second day.6 The undersides of all pangolins have no scales, just sparse fur. The four Asian species also have bristles growing between their scales, which is one way to tell them from African pangolins.6

Myth check: do scales have medicinal value?

Scales are keratin, the same material as your fingernails.6 Even so, they are the main driver of trafficking because of their use in traditional medicine.5 In 2025, China's official pharmacopoeia dropped all pangolin-based formulas.14

03 · Diversity

The eight species

There are four Asian species in the genus Manis, and four African species in Phataginus (tree pangolins) and Smutsia (ground pangolins). Every one of them is threatened with extinction.1

IUCN Red List categories are from the 2019 global assessments, which were the most recent as of 2025. The Pangolin Specialist Group was reassessing all eight species at that time.118 A possible ninth species, provisionally called Manis mysteria, was identified in 2023 from the DNA of scales seized in Hong Kong and Yunnan. It hasn't been formally described yet.11

04 · Ecology

Diet & behavior

Pangolins are insect specialists. Biologists call them myrmecophagous, meaning ant-eating.

70M+

Insects a year

One adult pangolin is estimated to eat more than 70 million insects a year, which makes pangolins important natural pest control.6

Ants & termites

Ants and termites are the staples. Pangolins sometimes add bee larvae, flies, worms, earthworms, and crickets. Because the diet is so specialized, pangolins are very hard to keep in captivity, and they often reject unfamiliar insects or get sick from them.6

Night-shift loners

Most species are solitary, nocturnal, and secretive, which makes them hard to study.6 The black-bellied pangolin is an exception. It is mostly active by day and lives almost entirely in trees.3

Diggers and climbers

Ground-dwelling species dig with their strong front legs while bracing on their tail and hind legs, and they kick loose soil a meter or more out of the burrow entrance. Others, like the Sunda and black-bellied pangolins, sleep in trees and use semi-prehensile tails to grip branches.6 The Sunda pangolin's tail is strong enough to hold its entire body weight.3

Pangolins mark their territories with urine, scent-gland secretions, and scattered feces. Scientists think the smells advertise dominance and breeding status.6 A single Chinese pangolin can dig 50 to 100 burrows a year.10

A slow life cycle

1 babyis the usual litter size46
~65–370 daysgestation range across species4
3–4 monthsof nursing; the baby rides on mom's tail6
~20 yearsreported lifespan in captivity6

Most species produce about one young per year,3 so populations recover very slowly from hunting.

05 · Distribution

Habitat & range

Pangolins live in tropical and flooded forests, thick brush, savanna grassland, and even cleared and farmed land. They generally occur wherever ants and termites are plentiful.6

Asia: 4 species

  • Indian: Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh
  • Chinese: southern China and Taiwan to Nepal and northeast India
  • Sunda: Myanmar and Thailand south through Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, and Indonesia
  • Philippine: the Palawan region of the Philippines only

Ranges from the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service and Sun et al.38

Africa: 4 species

  • White-bellied & black-bellied: West and Central African forests
  • Giant: equatorial Africa, from Senegal to Uganda and Tanzania
  • Temminck's: the most widespread, from South Africa through East Africa to southern Sudan and Chad

Ranges from USFWS and the African Pangolin Working Group.315

52%

The Chinese pangolin's potential range in eastern China shrank by 52.2% between the 1970s and the early 2000s. It now survives mainly in the Wuyi Mountains.17

57

Camera traps at 184 Chinese pangolin burrows (2020–2023) recorded 57 other vertebrate species using them, including birds, mammals, and a reptile.9

58 vs 47

In burned forests in Guangdong, sites with pangolin burrows had 58 plant species, compared with 47 at sites without burrows. They also had 35 animal species, compared with 23.10

2.4 m

Chinese pangolins are the only species known to overwinter. They dig winter burrows up to 2.4 m (8 ft) deep near termite nests.106

The takeaway is that pangolins are ecosystem engineers. Their digging turns and aerates soil, and their abandoned burrows become shelter for many other animals.10

06 · Threats

The world's most trafficked mammal

The UN Office on Drugs and Crime calls pangolins "arguably the most heavily trafficked wild mammal in the world."4 Demand comes mostly from Asia, where the meat is eaten as a delicacy and the scales are used in traditional medicine. Most of the pangolins trafficked today are African species smuggled to Asia.5

185 t

of pangolin scales were seized worldwide from 2014 to 2018, equal to about 370,000 pangolins. A single pangolin carries between 0.36 and 3.6 kg of scales.4

10×

increase in the number of whole-pangolin equivalents seized globally since 2014.4

~10%

Seizures may represent as little as this share of the real illegal trade, according to experts cited by WWF.5

Recent estimates of the scale of trafficking

Sources: [1] [4] [5]. In the 2017–2019 confiscations, WWF also counted 540,000 lb of scales. USFWS reports at least 269 tons of pangolin products confiscated worldwide from 2017 to 2021.3

Habitat loss

Forest loss and degradation compound the threat from overexploitation for all eight species.1

Snares & traps

At a rescue center in Taiwan, gin (leg-hold) traps caused 77.8% of trauma cases in pangolins.8

Dogs

Dog attacks were the second leading cause of trauma at the same center, accounting for 20.4% of cases, mostly tail injuries.8

Slow breeding

With one young at a time and long gestation, populations can't quickly replace animals that are lost.3

07 · Conservation

Fighting back: laws, rescues & research

Pangolin protection has grown over the past few decades. The record is mixed, but some places show that recovery is possible.

  1. 1989

    Taiwan's Wildlife Conservation Act

    Taiwan's pangolin population had collapsed after as many as 60,000 animals a year were harvested from 1950 to 1970. After this act passed, domestic consumption dropped significantly.8

  2. 2000

    Zero export quotas

    CITES set zero export quotas for the heavily depleted Asian species.4

  3. 2011

    Taiwan bans gin traps

    The Animal Protection Act banned making, selling, or using gin traps.8

  4. 2016

    CITES Appendix I

    At CoP17 in Johannesburg, all eight species were moved from Appendix II to Appendix I, the highest level of protection, which bans commercial international trade in wild pangolins. The listing took effect on January 2, 2017.27

  5. 2020

    China raises protection

    In June 2020, China gave the native Chinese pangolin its highest level of protection and stopped allowing raw pangolin scales in traditional medicine.5

  6. 2025

    Pharmacopoeia cleanup

    China's 2025 pharmacopoeia, effective October 1, 2025, removed 13 traditional formulas containing pangolin. An annual domestic quota of 1 metric ton of scales still remains.14

  7. 2025

    CITES CoP20

    An IUCN report prepared for CITES found that missing population data and reporting gaps make it hard to measure progress. Pangolins were on the agenda at the CITES meeting in Samarkand, Uzbekistan (Nov 24 to Dec 5, 2025).218

Did it work?

The results are mixed. USFWS reports "minimal evidence" that the Appendix I listing has reduced illegal trade.3 But Taiwan shows what sustained protection can do. Since the 1989 law, rescue centers and burrow surveys have recorded an increase in pangolins.8

60.7% → 88.5%
release rate of rescued pangolins in Taiwan8
35.9% → 10.7%
mortality of rescued pangolins8

Rescue in Vietnam

Save Vietnam's Wildlife reports 1,823 pangolins rescued and 1,019 released back to the wild, with a successful release rate above 70% (figures updated June 2026).12

08 · Did you know?

Fun facts

Hover over or tap a card to flip it.

FACT 01

Their closest relatives are carnivores

Tap to flip ↻

Pangolins aren't related to anteaters. Their closest living relatives are cats, dogs, and bears, and the two groups split almost 80 million years ago.5

FACT 02

Babies ride on mom's tail

Tap to flip ↻

Infants ride on the base of their mother's tail while she forages, and she curls around her baby when sleeping or when threatened.6

FACT 03

A new species found in seized scales

Tap to flip ↻

Genomes from seized scales revealed a possible ninth species, a fifth Asian pangolin that split from its relatives more than 5 million years ago.11

FACT 04

They swallow stones

Tap to flip ↻

Pangolins have no teeth. Small stones in their spiny, muscular stomach do the grinding instead.6

FACT 05

Burrows big enough to stand in

Tap to flip ↻

Some ground pangolin burrows have chambers large enough for a person to crawl in and stand up.6

FACT 06

Pangolins can swim

Tap to flip ↻

Despite their armor, pangolins are capable swimmers. They can also run surprisingly fast.6

FACT 07

Temminck's pangolin moves into other animals' burrows

Tap to flip ↻

Temminck's pangolins often use burrows dug by aardvarks and aardwolves.16

FACT 08

They have their own holiday

Tap to flip ↻

World Pangolin Day is held every February. In 2026 it fell on Saturday, February 21.13

09 · Take action

How you can help

You don't have to live near pangolins to help them.

1Never buy pangolin products

That includes scales, meat, leather, and medicines that contain them. Ask what's in traditional remedies before buying, and don't buy any wildlife product whose origin you can't verify.

2Report online listings

If you see pangolin products for sale online, report them through the Coalition to End Wildlife Trafficking Online's reporting form, or use the reporting links of its member companies.5

3Support boots on the ground

Donate to rescue centers and community-led projects such as Save Vietnam's Wildlife or the Pangolin Crisis Fund.1213

4Mark World Pangolin Day

Every February, share what you've learned, run a fundraiser, or host a talk at school or in your community.13

5Share accurate facts

Few people know pangolins exist, let alone that they're trafficked. When you share facts, cite reputable sources like the ones below.

6Travel responsibly

When traveling in Asia or Africa, avoid restaurants and markets that sell wild meat. Choose wildlife tours that don't let tourists handle animals.
